missed_cards.name: PR-LOCAL transcript forensics: usage-limit episodes, context growth, subagent share of tokens (6 to 20 Oct)
missed_cards.what_it_is: transcript_forensics.py, a read-only script that reports counts, timestamps and token figures only, scanned 9 main, 224 subagent and 26 journal transcripts of the clinic project slug. It produced summary.json, sessions.csv, limit_events.csv and api_limit_errors.csv. A verifier then checked 30 claims and tools/register_lane.py registered them (14 confirmed, 16 qualified). This is the only quantitative account in the testbed of how usage limits, subagents and context size interacted. No lane read it; A8 and A5 read only the SLM-LOCAL lane.
missed_cards.measured: Usage limit hit in at least 14 distinct episodes from 6 to 20 Oct; 104 error records, all five_hour (evidence.md PR-LOCAL-r1-01). Subagents and workflow agents made 82.4% of 4,155 API calls, 78.7% of output tokens and 62.4% of cache-read tokens, and 91 of the 104 limit records; one burst gave 40 limit records within 78 seconds (r1-03). The limit was typically reached about 75 minutes into the 5-hour window (median first-error-to-reset 224.7 min; range about 16 to 296 min) (r1-04). Main-session peak context: median 444,392, max 869,982; every main session started at 66,501 to 79,024 tokens (r1-05, summary.json main.peak_context_tokens and first_call_context_tokens). Zero compactions in 233 files (r1-07). Total about 778M tokens, 94.1% of them cache reads (731,972,373 cache read + 37,095,418 cache creation + 8,856,435 output + 8,356 input) (r1-23). Growth of the session 2d443524 was 69% the model's own retained output (thinking 31.5%, Write/Edit 21.3%) and repeated reads about 1% (r1-11).
missed_cards.limits: Covers 6 to 20 Oct under the OneDrive slug only, before the November build. The November transcripts (root 7f348b2c, 45 MB, 160 subagent files) were never analysed this way. How each token type counts toward plan limits is UNKNOWN (r1-23). Token figures elsewhere in the lane use chars/4, which the lane shows undercounts by about 25-35% here (r1-26).
missed_cards.transfer_to_fixflow: Highly transferable and cheap: the same script shape (dedupe assistant calls; per-session peak, first-call size, growth per call, limit errors per reset window) run over FixFlow's ~/.claude/projects transcripts would give the missing per-slice token and limit baseline. Its finding that subagent fan-out spends most of the limit and triggers the stops bears directly on how many parallel lanes a Pro or Max window can carry.

missed_cards.name: Workflow sizing for plan limits: tokens per 5-hour window, resume from disk state instead of resumeFromRunId, lean mode
missed_cards.what_it_is: Lessons from the three-project-deck workflow runs. A run of 10 parallel lanes died in about 15 minutes. The fix was lanes 2 at a time, every step writing to disk, tools/state.py computing what is finished and passing it as args.state, and no reliance on resumeFromRunId (its cache depends on call order, so a reordered lane re-ran a finished researcher). Stop starting agents after the first null result. Lean mode cut the per-claim refuter, critic and judge layers to one verifier per lane plus a script registrar.
missed_cards.measured: Run 1: stopped by the 5-hour limit after about 15 minutes at 2.44M subagent tokens; 2 of 19 agents finished (WORKFLOW.md run log row 1). Resume with lanes 2 at a time: 30 minutes, 3.4M subagent tokens, 48 agents, 18 finished (row 2). Lean run: 30 of 31 agents finished on 3.28M subagent tokens; 10 of 10 lanes and 167 claims registered (row 4). Deck-and-audit run: 4 of 4 agents, 0.80M (row 5). 'one window covered only about 3.4M subagent tokens' (WORKFLOW.md:67); each full window used about 14% of the weekly limit (pro-plan-workflow-limits.md:17).
missed_cards.limits: Measured on the Pro plan in October with a Workflow-tool script, not with the November session tree. It gives no unattended resume after a limit; a human still relaunches. Lean mode trades rigour for completion, and the slide layer was not re-audited (row 6).
missed_cards.transfer_to_fixflow: Directly reusable for FixFlow workflows: budget each run in subagent tokens per window before launch, checkpoint every agent's output to disk, resume from a state file rather than the run cache, and cap concurrent lanes.

missed_cards.name: Migration numbering across parallel slices and the migration-graph test

missed_cards.name: Windows-host tooling traps that produced false passes or wasted rounds
missed_cards.what_it_is: Recorded traps of the shared Windows PC and the desktop app's shell. (1) grep -c $'\r' reports every line as a CR match, so 'verified 0 CR' checks were right by luck and the root's own check wrongly flagged clean files; use git ls-files --eol. (2) A Python open(p,'w') writes CRLF and turns a four-line edit into a whole-file diff (found in S11 in five files). (3) Long Bash heredocs with quotes fail with 'unexpected EOF'. (4) Parallel sessions overwrite and delete generic log names in $TEMP. (5) Hyper-V refuses disk files under %LOCALAPPDATA%; the session is not elevated, so each elevated call needs a UAC click; Secure Boot blocks the Debian image; a VM hangs at first boot; every reboot powers the VM off and moves the Default Switch subnet.
missed_cards.measured: The rerun cost a 16-minute check (shared-temp-clobbers-logs.md:11); 'each of these cost 10-40 minutes of blind retries' (hyperv-rig-gotchas.md:19); a VM hung at first boot in 3 of 3 creations (hyperv-rig-gotchas.md:23).
missed_cards.limits: Recorded as memory and process notes; no check enforces them, except LF, which the repository's hook and git --eol checks partly enforce.
missed_cards.transfer_to_fixflow: Same PC, same app shell: FixFlow sessions should write logs to the session scratchpad, verify line endings with git ls-files --eol, and write scripts with the Write tool rather than heredocs. These are cheap rules to put in FixFlow's CLAUDE.md.

critic.closest_to_owner_recollection: The clinic repository (main and every branch) holds no SQLite graph-based library and nothing that makes the repository evolve by itself. The only SQLite graph code in it is vendored third-party evidence: claude-context-hooks reads a cairn-graph code-structure graph.db (output/corpus-map-justification/10-context-admission-research/sources/claude-context-hooks/hooks/lib/cairn_graph_footer.py). The project's own nearest things are: (1) the corpus map, a typed-edge graph of the planning documents stored as JSONL with a coverage ledger and a hash-based refresh command, whose validation trial was never run; (2) tools/context_system, compaction-steering hooks with exact lexical recall over transcripts, which were never installed and whose only measured token result is a 6 to 17 percent increase; (3) the root session's agent-written memory folder outside the repository, a failure-driven lesson store loaded into later sessions (CR-01); and (4) research notes on external SQLite or DAG memory systems (LCM, Virtual Context, Cairn, Headroom), none adopted. The best match to 'SQLite graph-based library ... faster recall that minimises token use' is in FixFlow, not the clinic: the knowledge-store design on FixFlow PR #183 (v1.3.1) chose SQLite via node:sqlite as the query engine over an append-only journal, with a grafted topology, so cheap agents can find past diagnoses instead of re-solving them. That design is unbuilt and its owner step D1 (run the audit) is still open.
